title: The five remembrances again
hookLine: five lines for anyone, householder or monk: aging, sickness, death, parting, and heir to my deeds (AN 5.57)
tomorrow: a mother searches for one mustard seed. what does she find?

lines: A LIST ON THE LOCK SCREEN.
cards: Some people keep a short list on the lock screen: three goals, a verse, a reminder to drink water.
The Buddha gave a list to recite often, and he said it was for everyone: a woman or a man, a householder or someone who has left home. Five lines.
They come back today, because this week has been walking right through them.

teach.b: Here they are, from the Anguttara Nikaya, in plain words. I will grow old; I can't escape aging. I can get sick; I can't escape illness.
I will die; I can't escape death.
Everyone and everything dear to me will change, and I'll be parted from them.

teach.h: THE FIFTH: MY DEEDS ARE MY OWN.
teach.b: And the fifth: my deeds are my own. I'm the heir to my deeds; whatever I do, good or bad, I'll inherit it. The Buddha gives each line a reason.
The first three loosen pride in youth, health and life. The fourth loosens grabbing at what we love. The fifth turns a person toward what they do.
Now look back at the week inside them. The weaver's daughter: no one knows when. Nagarjuna's bubble in the wind: fragile.
Food and medicine: few supports. The third root: only the practice. The burning house: it stays behind.
And the body: even the body.
Every one of those is folded into the five. The first four name what can't be held.
The last names what's left in your hands: heir to my deeds.

how: Buddhist communities in several traditions recite the five remembrances in daily chanting, in Pali or in translation; Theravada monasteries and some Zen and Plum Village communities include them in their regular services.

games.q: what does “the five remembrances again” mean?
o: five people to remember in prayer each morning
five lines on aging, illness, death, parting, deeds
five rules a monk recites on joining the order

games.q: the five, and what each loosens — tap the pairs.
p: loosens grabbing at what we love
turns a person toward what they do

s: the Buddha gave the five remembrances only to monks and nuns
he said a woman or a man, a householder or one who has left home, should recall them often.
the fifth remembrance says whatever i do, good or bad, i'll inherit it
i'm the heir to my deeds: the one line about what's still in your hands.

games.q: a friend says the five remembrances sound depressing: 'four lines of bad news.' which line answers her best?
o: the third: death is the most important one to remember.
the fifth: after naming what can't be held, it names what's in your hands.
none; the list is meant to be hard, so she should push through.
games.why: the first four loosen grabbing; the fifth turns a person toward what they do: heir to my deeds.

practice: Say the five aloud, slowly, once: I will grow old; I can get sick; I will die; I'll be parted from all that's dear; I'm the heir to my deeds. Then sit with whichever line stayed with you, and let the others rest.

wordCard.voice: The five remembrances: aging, illness, death, parting, and heir to my deeds. Five lines the Buddha said anyone should recall often.

orig.note: Pali: kamma (Sanskrit karma), deeds; the fifth remembrance calls a person the heir to their kamma.

carryVoice: The line to keep: heir to my deeds, the one thing still in your hands. Two weeks of remembering, closed with five lines.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.57 (Upajjhatthana Sutta: five subjects to reflect on often, with the reason for each, for women and men, householders and those gone forth)
